title: The 2 Players' Problem: mean, median and mode side by side
summary: Working the professor's two-player runs data through the mean, median and mode, and reading all three on one dot plot.

chunks.heading: The data, and the same mean twice
chunks.explanation_md:
The slide gives the **runs scored by two players in different matches**, 20 matches each:

- **Player-1:** 78, 2, 67, 45, 8, 0, 4, 78, 90, 3, 12, 12, 56, 3, 4, 5, 90, 90, 4, 4
- **Player-2:** 45, 25, 35, 45, 27, 45, 32, 45, 26, 30, 28, 31, 32, 38, 37, 26, 26, 27, 28, 27

Start with the **mean**, X̄ = Σxᵢ / n, with n = 20 for each player.

**Player-1:** Σxᵢ = 655, so X̄ = 655 / 20 = **32.75**

**Player-2:** Σxᵢ = 655, so X̄ = 655 / 20 = **32.75**

Same total, same mean. If you only looked at the average, the two players would look identical. Now look at the raw numbers again: they clearly are not.
chunks.exam_line: Both players' runs add to the same total, so the mean alone cannot tell the two players apart.

check_questions.stem: Using X̄ = Σxᵢ / n on the 20 scores, what is Player-1's mean?
Player-1 and Player-2 have the same mean runs.
check_questions.explanation: Both sets of scores add to 655, and 655 / 20 = 32.75 for each.

chunks.heading: Mean and median: the first question
chunks.explanation_md:
The next slide repeats the tables and asks: **"What is observation made by you from Mean and Median?"**

**Median** (n = 20 is even, so average the (n/2)th and (n/2 + 1)th terms, the 10th and 11th):

- Player-1 in ascending order: 0, 2, 3, 3, 4, 4, 4, 4, 5, **8**, **12**, 12, 45, 56, 67, 78, 78, 90, 90, 90. Median = (8 + 12)/2 = **10**
- Player-2 in ascending order: 25, 26, 26, 26, 27, 27, 27, 28, 28, **30**, **31**, 32, 32, 35, 37, 38, 45, 45, 45, 45. Median = (30 + 31)/2 = **30.5**

**What the numbers show:**

- Player-1: mean 32.75 but median only 10. In half of the matches Player-1 scored 8 runs or fewer; a handful of big scores (90, 90, 90, 78, 78, 67, 56) lift the mean.
- Player-2: mean 32.75 and median 30.5, close together. All scores sit between 25 and 45.

This is the median slide's point in action: **a few extremely large values can inflate the mean**, and **whenever a data set has extreme values, the median is the preferred measure of central location**.
chunks.exam_line: Same mean, very different medians: Player-1's few big scores inflate the mean, so the median shows the typical score better.

check_questions.stem: The slide asking for your observation from the mean and median prints its own answer.
check_questions.explanation: It only asks the question; you work out the answer.

chunks.heading: Adding the mode: the second question
chunks.explanation_md:
The third version of the slide asks: **"What is observation made by you from Mean, Median and Mode?"**

**Mode** (the value with the greatest frequency):

- Player-1: **4** appears four times (90 appears three times). Mode = **4**.
- Player-2: **45** appears four times (26 and 27 appear three times each). Mode = **45**.

Put the three measures together:

| | Mean | Median | Mode |
|---|---|---|---|
| Player-1 | 32.75 | 10 | 4 |
| Player-2 | 32.75 | 30.5 | 45 |

The means match, but the median and mode tell very different stories about the two players. The deck asks you to look at all three, not just the average.
chunks.exam_line: Both players have the same mean but very different medians and modes, so the three measures can tell different stories.

chunks.heading: Mean, median and mode on one dot plot
chunks.explanation_md:
This slide shows all three measures on one picture.

**TABLE 1-2** lists each data value with its frequency: **18 (4)**, 19 (1), 20 (3), 21 (1), 22 (2), 23 (1), 24 (1), 26 (1), 27 (1), 32 (1), 33 (1), 49 (1), 52 (1), 56 (1).

The **dot plot** stacks one dot per value on an axis from 18 to 56, and marks:

- **Mode** under **18**: the tallest stack, four dots (greatest frequency).
- **Median** under the 22 area.
- **Mean (26.9)** between 26 and 28.

Check the mean yourself: the frequencies add to 20 values, and the values add to 538, so 538 / 20 = **26.9**.

Look at where the dots sit: most between 18 and 33, and three far to the right at **49, 52 and 56**. The mean is the measure furthest to the right. Link it back to the median slide: a few extremely large values can inflate the mean.
chunks.exam_line: On the Table 1-2 dot plot: Mode at 18, Median near 22, Mean 26.9, with three large values (49, 52, 56) far to the right.

questions.model_answer_md:
**Formula:** X̄ = Σxᵢ / n, with n = 20 matches for each player.

**Player-1:** adding five matches at a time: 200 + 175 + 87 + 193 = **655**. X̄ = 655 / 20 = **32.75**

**Player-2:** 177 + 178 + 166 + 134 = **655**. X̄ = 655 / 20 = **32.75**

questions.model_answer_md:
**Mode:** 18, which has the greatest frequency (4) and the tallest stack of dots.

**Median:** n = 20, so average the 10th and 11th values; both are 22, so the median is **22**.

**Mean:** Σxᵢ = 538, so 538 / 20 = **26.9**, as labelled on the plot.

**Order:** Mode (18) < Median (22) < Mean (26.9). Most dots sit between 18 and 33, but **three values far to the right (49, 52, 56)** pull the mean up. As the median slide says, **a few extremely large values can inflate the mean**; the median and mode are not pulled the same way.

questions.stem: 'What is observation made by you from Mean, Median and Mode?' Answer the slide's question for the 2 Players' Problem with full working for all three measures.
questions.model_answer_md:
The slide gives 20 match scores for each player and asks what the three measures reveal.

**1. Mean (X̄ = Σxᵢ / n)**
- Player-1: Σxᵢ = 655, X̄ = 655 / 20 = **32.75**
- Player-2: Σxᵢ = 655, X̄ = 655 / 20 = **32.75**

**2. Median (n = 20 is even: average the 10th and 11th terms)**
- Player-1 sorted: 0, 2, 3, 3, 4, 4, 4, 4, 5, **8, 12**, 12, 45, 56, 67, 78, 78, 90, 90, 90. Median = (8 + 12)/2 = **10**
- Player-2 sorted: 25, 26, 26, 26, 27, 27, 27, 28, 28, **30, 31**, 32, 32, 35, 37, 38, 45, 45, 45, 45. Median = (30 + 31)/2 = **30.5**

**3. Mode (greatest frequency)**
- Player-1: 4 appears four times (90 three times). Mode = **4**
- Player-2: 45 appears four times (26 and 27 three times each). Mode = **45**

| | Mean | Median | Mode |
|---|---|---|---|
| Player-1 | 32.75 | 10 | 4 |
| Player-2 | 32.75 | 30.5 | 45 |

**Observations:**
- **Same mean, different players.** On the average alone they look identical.
- **Player-1 is erratic.** In half the matches Player-1 scored 8 or fewer, and the most common score is 4. A handful of big scores (90, 90, 90, 78, 78, 67, 56) lift the mean far above the typical score. This is the slide's warning: **a few extremely large values can inflate the mean**, so with extreme values **the median is the preferred measure**.
- **Player-2 is consistent.** Mean 32.75 and median 30.5 are close, and every score lies between 25 and 45.

**Conclusion:** looking at all three measures, not just the mean, shows Player-2 is the steadier performer and Player-1 depends on occasional big innings.

rubric.point: Player-1's big scores inflate the mean; median preferred with extreme values
Player-2 consistent; look at all three measures

questions.stem: Using the percentile index rule, find Q1, Q3 and the interquartile range of each player's runs in the 2 Players' Problem. What do the IQRs add to the mean, median and mode?
questions.model_answer_md:
Quartiles are specific percentiles: **Q1 = 25th**, **Q3 = 75th**. Index rule: **i = (p/100) x n**; if i is an integer, average the ith and (i + 1)th values.

- Q1: i = (25/100) x 20 = 5, so average the 5th and 6th values.
- Q3: i = (75/100) x 20 = 15, so average the 15th and 16th values.

**Sorted scores:**
- Player-1: 0, 2, 3, 3, **4, 4**, 4, 4, 5, 8, 12, 12, 45, 56, **67, 78**, 78, 90, 90, 90
- Player-2: 25, 26, 26, 26, **27, 27**, 27, 28, 28, 30, 31, 32, 32, 35, **37, 38**, 45, 45, 45, 45

| | Q1 | Q3 | IQR = Q3 - Q1 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Player-1 | (4 + 4)/2 = **4** | (67 + 78)/2 = **72.5** | **68.5** |
| Player-2 | (27 + 27)/2 = **27** | (37 + 38)/2 = **37.5** | **10.5** |

**What the IQRs add:**
- The **IQR measures the spread of the middle 50%** of the data and is useful for **understanding data variability**.
- Player-1's middle half of scores runs from 4 to 72.5, a spread of 68.5 runs: very unpredictable.
- Player-2's middle half runs from 27 to 37.5, a spread of only 10.5 runs: very steady.
- The mean (32.75 for both) could not show this at all; the median and mode hinted at it, and the IQR measures it directly.

**Conclusion:** same mean, but Player-1's IQR is more than six times Player-2's, so Player-2 is clearly the more consistent player.

rubric.point: Q1 = 25th, Q3 = 75th percentile; i = 5 and i = 15
IQR measures spread of the middle 50%
Same mean hides very different variability; Player-2 more consistent
